title: How Well Do You Tolerate Ambiguity
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post describes tolerance for ambiguity as a distinguishing trait among leaders: some stay calm and build flexible plans when information is incomplete, while others rush to resolve the uncertainty. The author cites psychology's view that high tolerance is linked to better decisions, creativity, emotional intelligence, openness to new ideas and lower stress. Whether the trait is innate or learned is left unresolved, but the practical advice assumes it can be grown through repeated experience making decisions under uncertainty. A decades-old self-report scale by Stanley Budner is offered as a way to gauge where one stands. The closing claim is that leading mostly means not knowing, and that getting comfortable with this is a lifelong task.
points: Leaders with high tolerance for ambiguity wait for outcomes to become more predictable instead of forcing early decisions.
The trait is associated with stronger decision-making, creativity, emotional intelligence and resilience, and with lower stress.
Because tolerance is built through practice, seeking out more decisions made under uncertain conditions is the prescribed training method.
A long-standing self-assessment (Budner's scale) gives leaders a baseline measure of their own tolerance.
quotes: When clarity and certainty remain elusive, some leaders shine. As conditions change rapidly, these leaders relax and take it all in.

When information is unclear or incomplete, they formulate a flexible game plan. They engage uncertainty with an inner confidence and patience to allow the situation to unwind naturally. They refuse to jump the gun and make decisions until the possible outcomes become more predictable.

Learning to tolerate ambiguity is associated with a host of positive and related qualities and outcomes. Leaders with a high tolerance for ambiguity tend to be better decision-makers, more creative problem-solvers, higher in emotional intelligence, active innovators, and more open to new ideas and experiences.

The debate as to whether leaders are born with this tolerance or if they come to develop it over time is unlikely to be settled any time soon. But if you’re generally in the camp of nurture over nature, then the practical advice for enhancing your tolerance for ambiguity begins with increasing your experience as a problem-solver and decision-maker. The more opportunities you find for making decisions during uncertain situations, the more tolerance you will build.

More than 60 years ago, psychologist Stanley Budner developed a self-report scale that attempted to measure a leader’s tolerance for ambiguity. This self-assessment remains popular and still provides a useful lens into how much tolerance for ambiguity a given leader has.

No matter how well or poorly you score, working on becoming even more tolerant of ambiguity is a worthy goal for any leader. Learning to lead with ambiguity is about embracing the reality of organizational life.
